The 4 denials all had a visible financial risk factor. Two had high debt-to-income ratios (>60% and 50%-60%). One had a loan-to-value ratio above 100% (100.205). One had a 47% DTI with $64k income. Comparable high-DTI or high-LTV applications from White, Hispanic, Black, and Asian male applicants were also commonly denied. Many Asian female applicants with DTI in the 40s and LTV of 80-98% were approved. Confidence is not higher for three reasons: the data lacks credit scores and other underwriting variables, the counts are approximate, and this pattern cannot rule out discrimination in factors not captured here.

Asian female applicants appear in roughly 100+ rows, and only about 7 were denied, a denial rate of roughly 6-7%. These are approximate hand counts, not exact figures. That rate is similar to or slightly below the overall denial rate (about 8-9%) and below the rates for some other groups, such as Hispanic or Latino and White female applicants. At least 3 of the 7 denied Asian female applicants had debt-to-income ratios above 60%, and another had a loan-to-value ratio near 99-100%. These are standard risk factors that plausibly explain those denials. Most Asian female applicants, including those with high incomes, moderate DTI and LTV values around 80%, were approved. The data shows no pattern of worse outcomes for Asian females than for comparable applicants. However, the sample of Asian female denials is small, and key underwriting variables such as credit score are not in the data. This limits how firmly discrimination can be ruled out.
